etymologies.etymologyHTML: Inherited from Middle English blundren, blondren (verb) and blunder, blonder (“disturbance, strife”), from the verb; partly from Middle English blondren, a frequentative form of Middle English blonden, blanden ("to mix; mix up"; corresponding to blend +‎ -er); and partly from Middle English blundren, a frequentative form of Middle English blunden (“to stagger; stumble”), from Old Norse blunda (“to shut the eyes; doze”). Cognates include Norwegian blunda (“to shut the eyes; doze”), dialectal Swedish blundra (“to act blindly or rashly”), Danish blunde (“to blink”) or blunde (“to take a nap”), Icelandic blunda (“to nap; doze”). Related to English blind.

definitions.definition: (chess) A very bad move, usually caused by some tactical oversight.
(intransitive) To make a clumsy or stupid mistake.

quote.citation: October 6, 1759, Oliver Goldsmith, The Bee No. 1
quote.text: I was never distinguished for address, and have often even blundered in making my bow.

quote.citation: 1700, [John] Dryden, “Palamon and Arcite: Or, The Knight’s Tale. In Three Books.”, in Fables Ancient and Modern; […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: blunders on, and staggers every pace

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause to make a mistake.

quote.citation: 1714, Humphry Ditton, A discourse concerning the resurrection of Jesus Christ:

definitions.definition: (transitive) To do or treat in a blundering manner; to confuse.

quote.citation: 1676, Edward Stillingfleet, A Defence of the Discourse Concerning the Idolatry Practised in the Church of Rome:
quote.text: He blunders and confounds all these together.

definitions.definition: (chess, intransitive) To make a very bad move.
(chess, transitive) To make a very bad move and thereby cause the loss of (a piece).
